title: Low-Dose Aspirin Does Not Reduce Cancer Incidence in Women Cook NR, Lee IM, Gaziano JM, et al. Low-dose aspirin in the primary prevention of cancer: the Women's Health Study: a randomized controlled trial. JAMA 2005;294:47-55.

sections.abstract: specific cancers, the RR was 0.98 (95% CI, 0.87‐1.09; P = 0.68) for breast cancer, 0.97 (95% CI, 0.77‐1.24; P = 0.83) for colorectal cancer, and 0.78 (95% CI, 0.59‐1.03; P = 0.08) for lung cancer. There were no statistically significant differences seen between the groups for total cancer-related mortality or any site-specific cancer-related mortality, with the exception of lung cancer (RR, 0.70 [95% CI, 0.50‐0.99; P = 0.04]). There was a total of 2510 self-reported colon polyps in the aspirin group as compared with 2578 in the placebo group (RR, 0.97 [95% CI, 0.92‐1.02; P = 0.27]). There were no statistically significant differences in aspirin’s effect on cancer incidence when stratified by age, body mass index, alcohol use, physical activity, menopausal status, hormone therapy, or family history of cancer. Conclusion . Low-dose aspirin does not reduce the incidence of cancer after 10 years of therapy. Low-does aspirin may reduce lung cancer‐related deaths, but this effect was small.
